Theodore Roosevelt's second inauguration. On March 4, 1905, Theodore Roosevelt delivered an address confirming his ascent to the presidency in his own right after assuming office following William McKinley's assassination in 1901. His election in 1904 made him the first president elected solely in his own right after succession. At 46, Roosevelt delivered an address emphasizing America's role as a world power and the Square Deal ideology. The Square Deal represented fair labor, conservation, and corporate regulation that balanced the interests of capital and labor. Roosevelt declared America's duty as a great power to maintain order and civilization in its sphere of influence. He highlighted conservation of natural resources, a signature initiative that would reshape American environmental policy. He called for honest dealing in government and business, contrasting sharply with the corruption that had marked the Gilded Age. Roosevelt's address reflected his famous philosophy: speak softly and carry a big stick. He emphasized personal vigor and national strength, positioning the United States as a global imperial power maintaining order especially in Latin America and the Pacific. His vision shaped American foreign policy and domestic progressivism for a generation.
